lessons.t: Wealth Roadmap — taught by Sharran Srivatsaa (Acquisition.com / ACQ Ventures)
lessons.md: Educational only — not individual financial, tax or legal advice. Sharran's background: ex-Goldman Sachs banker, built two companies worth $1B+, five exits, ~29 investments in 12 months at ACQ Ventures, $500M+ ACQ real-estate portfolio.

lessons.t: Wealth 1 — Start Here: the 5 Money Milestones (7 min)
lessons.md:
- Problem: people work hard and earn money but get only vague tactics ("max your 401k", "$1k emergency fund", "buy ETFs", "pay off the house") and **no sequence**. So business owners just keep pouring everything back into the business.
- **M-O-N-E-Y**, each milestone unlocking the next:
- **M — Margin**: active income > monthly expenses, so you stop falling behind.
- **O — Optionality**: a transition fund of 6–12 months of essential expenses, so if income stops you have time to reinvent yourself.
- **N — Net financial assets of $100k**: the point where your money starts earning money while you sleep.
- **E — Equity rich**: $1M net worth excluding your primary home. In the US this is the accredited-investor bar, which opens private deals.
- **Y — Your terms**: passive income > monthly expenses. This is real financial freedom, not a jet or a vanity number.
- Work **one milestone at a time** and finish each lesson's action step. "Money loves speed, but wealth loves time."

- **Margin = active income − monthly expenses.** It's the raw material for every later milestone. You can't invest your way out of a cash-flow problem. Active income (trading skill for pay) isn't bad: LeBron and Elon both earn it.
- Example: $5,000 net income − $4,600 spending = $400 margin. The goal is **repeatable** margin every month.
- **3 levers**:
- **Know your expenses.** Upload ~3 months of card and bank statements to AI and ask for monthly totals by category (housing, transport, food, debt, subscriptions, misc). Your "monthly nut" carries through every milestone.
- **Cut or optimize the big ones.** Moving to save $400/month in rent doubles that $400 margin, about $4.8k a year. One big decision beats dozens of tiny cuts (nobody got rich skipping lattes).
- **Increase active income**, the lever with no ceiling (cutting has a floor). Options: offer more value and ask for a raise, change jobs, learn a higher-value skill, side income, or **raise prices** in your business (most workshop businesses are badly underpriced).
- Story: Sharran's college roommate needed $65k for his Chicago doorman apartment and Honda. When his sister fell ill and moved in, he needed about $120k, so he got a project-management certificate in ~90 days and landed a $120k job. Don't wait for a crisis to force your growth.
- **Lifestyle inflation is the silent killer**: expenses rising with income leaves margin at zero, as with LA's "$100 millionaires" who live rich but hold nothing.
- **Actions**: download 30 days of statements → have AI compute monthly expenses → pick one lever. **Milestone complete: consistent margin for 90 days.**

- The biggest emergency isn't a flat tyre; it's **losing your income**. Replace the $1,000 "emergency fund" with a **transition fund** that gives you time to reinvent yourself. Small surprises can come from margin or a credit card.
- **Target = essential monthly expenses × 6** (up to 12). Count essentials only: housing, transport, food, utilities, insurance, minimum debt payments. Example: $5k/month gives a $30k target; $4k/month gives $24k for 6 months or $48k for 12.
- **Keep it in a separate account** so it doesn't get spent: liquid, low risk, keeping pace with inflation (high-yield savings or money market). **Automate a fixed transfer** on payday or distribution day. $1,000/month reaches $24k in 24 months, and there's no need to rush.
- **Actions**: calculate the target → open a separate account → schedule the first automated transfer. **Complete: 6 months of essential expenses saved.** After that you can play offense.

lessons.t: Wealth 4 — Milestone 3: $100k Net Financial Assets (17 min)
lessons.md:
- **Net financial assets** = financial assets (things that grow, pay you or can be sold for cash) − debt against them. Example: $130k − $30k = $100k. Don't count the transition fund.
- **The first $100k is the slowest.** At $2k/month and 10% growth, the first $100k takes ~42 months, the second ~31 and the third ~25. Left alone, $100kcompoundsto~$260k in about 10 years. Pace by monthly contribution: $1k → ~8 years, $2k → ~4.2 years, $3k → ~2.8 years. **Front-load the effort** with short-term sacrifices, then you can slow down later.
- **Three parts**:
- **Freeze your lifestyle.** When income rises, keep spending flat and invest the difference. Sharran's family lived on his wife's Deloitte salary for 2+ years while his real-estate company made nothing. They still run the household on the same monthly nut they had 14 years ago, while net worth grew 50×+. He doesn't even wear a watch.
- **Build a "money factory"**: active income (W-2, 1099, course sales, LLC) flows into one structure (typically a living trust) → lifestyle (fixed monthly nut + tax savings) → **surplus** → passive investments that grow and pay income.
- **Measure net worth monthly.** Build a personal balance sheet listing everything you own and owe (401k, IRA, brokerage, HSA, cash). Upload statements to AI each month. Banks (e.g. SBA loans) ask for this statement first. "You can't grow what you don't measure."
- **TIGA (tiny income-generating asset)**: start with ~$100/month. His 15-year-old son holds SCHD (Schwab dividend ETF) and was amazed by his first ~$30 dividend that arrived while he was in school.
- Order of dollars: take any 401k **employer match** (an instant 100% return), then mostly a taxable brokerage account for least friction toward $100k.
- **Business-owner trap**: a business returning $10 for every $1 of ads tempts you to reinvest everything, but your personal wealth also has to compound. "A business that works isn't the same as a life that works."
- Buffett: if you don't find a way to make money while you sleep, you'll work until you die.
- **Actions**: build the net-worth statement → set a monthly investment amount → open the account. **Complete: $100k NFA, proven by the statement.**

lessons.t: Wealth 5 — Milestone 4: Equity Rich ($1M net worth ex-home) (19 min)
lessons.md:
- **Why $1M**: it's the US **accredited investor** threshold (net worth excluding primary residence). Below it you're locked out of private deals, which require verification. The game is **access to deal flow the public never sees**, not influencer ETF picks.
- **The "golden stairways": business and real estate.** They dominate the Forbes 400, the US tax code favours real estate, and both give **equity**, meaning **asymmetric upside**.
- **4 routes to $1M**:
- **Grow your business's value** by optimizing whatever it's valued on (ARR for tech, EBITDA multiple otherwise). Run it as if it's for sale, even if you only "sell it back to yourself" every year.
- **Take distributions** and deploy them outside the business, tax-efficiently, instead of shoving everything back in.
- **Public markets** (stocks, ETFs, bonds, treasuries): accessible, regulated and liquid. **Invest on a schedule.** His son owns VNQ (real-estate ETF) as a TIGA.
- **Tax advantages**: accounts (IRA, 401k, SEP, defined-benefit, HSA) and **location**. Online workers can leave California (~13.1% state tax) for FL/TX/NV (0%) — effectively a 13% raise. Puerto Rico has a low flat rate.
- **The 4 money monsters**:
- **Inflation**: $100k at 1.5% for 20 years grows to ~$134k while prices rise 3–4%. Sharran's own cash-management mix is equal parts SGOV (T-bills), SCHO (short treasuries), TIP (inflation-protected) and SCHD (dividends). He's "allergic" to idle cash in checking and sweeps surplus there every month. That's a model, not advice; a high-yield savings account works too.
- **Taxes**, the #1 drag: **separate the tax *preparer (compliance, filing) from a tax strategist*** (forward planning, one or two big ideas, stands behind you in an audit). This is what the wealthiest families do.
- **Interruption** (emotion): over the 30 years to 2015 the S&P returned ~10%/year while the average investor got ~3.6% ($100k→~$293k instead of ~$1.9M). Fix it with **written rules** (e.g. "if the market drops 20%, I invest more / don't touch it").
- **Fees**: $1M at 10% for 20 years ≈ $6.6M; a 1% fee costs over $1M. Ask every advisor **how they get paid**.
- **Actions**: use tax-advantaged accounts and location → beat the four monsters → reach $1M net worth ex-home on your statement.

lessons.t: Wealth 6 — Milestone 5: Living Life on Your Terms (14 min)
lessons.md:
- **Financial freedom = passive income > monthly expenses.** Working becomes an option, not an obligation, and you can wake up asking "what would I like to do today?" It isn't a bank-balance number or "retire at 65".
- **Passive income is pre-funded**, either with effort (a startup or affiliate work that pays over time) or with money (dividend stocks, private credit, rental real estate). Start by experiencing a first dividend through a simple dividend portfolio.
- **Track one number, the coverage ratio = passive income ÷ monthly expenses.** Example: $6k ÷ $26k ≈ 23%. Watch it climb to 33%, 50%, 100%+. Above 100% you're "truly abundant".
- Sharran holds under 5% of his net worth in the S&P and the rest in private investments. The S&P averages ~10% but swings widely year to year; he cites private markets as averaging ~55% higher returns, with more risk.
- **Three private buckets**:
- **Private credit** (his favourite): lend to companies that can't get bank loans. You sit high in the capital stack and collect interest, so you're the bank.
- **Private equity**: own part of someone else's private company.
- **Real estate** (~55% of his net worth): pays monthly, has tax benefits, can be borrowed against, and has basic demand (everyone needs housing). You can borrow up to ~80%, contribute ~20% and keep the cash flow after debt service.
- **His one redo: multifamily over single-family.** After 190+ single-family homes, he notes that single-family value depends on neighbouring comps, while multifamily is valued like a business on **NOI** (net operating income), so better operation means more value. ACQ owns ~3,600 units across the US Southeast. Proceeds from Alex's record book launch (~$106M in 72 hours) went into the business and multifamily.
- **Access**: (1) invest **in groups or funds** (often accredited only, ~$100k minimums); (2) back **operators**, the active people doing the work, while you're the passive capital partner.
- **Actions**: calculate your coverage % now → pick one private deal type (credit or real estate) and learn it **in a group first** (you learn 10× faster) → aim for over 100%. **Complete: coverage ratio over 100%.**

videos.md:
## Money, Wealth & Investing

203 ideas from 98 videos. [#N] = video N in the Start here tab.

- Volume is capped by time and physical limits; leverage is not. The goal is to out-leverage competitors rather than out-work them (better skill, tools, lists, timing, offer, recorded/broadcast pitches, and finally other people working for you). [▶ 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RdAKXJlMIZM)
- There is no truly passive income, only less-active income: everyone trades time for money, so the real question is how much you get back per hour invested. [▶ 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RdAKXJlMIZM)
- Owning beats earning: to earn $1M net you need roughly $2M pre-tax income saved over years (e.g. $200k/yr for a decade), while a self-running business making $250k profit could sell at around 4x for $1M almost as soon as it is built. [▶ 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VBoRLJimVzc)
- Pay yourself some cash to force cash flow and build a reserve; options include a 33% to you / 33% growth / 33% reserves split, or a "watermark" where you keep enough for planned growth and distribute the rest. [▶ 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VBoRLJimVzc)
- Get rich once: take big risks with small money, small risks with big money. Remove the "genius with 1,000 hands" by building systems and people so the business has enterprise value (e.g. $2M profit at a 5-7x multiple). Market in four directions: prospects, customers, candidates and employees. [▶ 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VBoRLJimVzc)
- When broke with low skills, your only asset is time, so the goal is to free up time to learn a valuable skill while still providing. Cut every cost for a season: no eating out, discount groceries only, no new clothes for two years, and live with family or share housing with others saving too. [▶ 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YFA8AS5Cu2w)
- If you have under $100k saved, go fully defensive so you can later afford bets (education, software, inventory): discount groceries only, thrift-store clothes, only free social events, and spend spare time applying for better jobs, side work and higher-paid skills. Once your hourly earning power is high (e.g. $500 per 30 minutes selling), outsource anything worth less than that. [▶ 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aFoMYz_jWcs)
- To impress poor people, outspend them; to impress rich people, outwork them. Live far below your means so you can pounce on bigger opportunities; his $1.7M house was bought in cash from one month's income, and a Bentley he bought under pressure was returned at a $20k loss. [▶ 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aFoMYz_jWcs)
- Money is stored time; wealth measures how little of your life you must trade for what you want. Leverage multiplies time, and opportunity size scales with the leverage you can use. Passive income is overrated; what people really want is options and engaging work. [▶ 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qxQIcDrre1E)
- Index funds and real estate held long-term are a safe way to grow money (day trading is not), but putting spare cash into passive assets early can signal you have stopped trying to raise your income. [▶ 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dZ7xeVCYC5M)
- Your earning capacity is your biggest investment: e.g. a 2-day, ~$500 phlebotomy certification could take someone from minimum wage to about $25/hour, roughly tripling income for life. [▶ 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dZ7xeVCYC5M)
- Live as cheaply as possible and put 100% of the surplus into education that raises earnings: on $50k/year, living on $20k leaves about $2k/month for courses, coaching, mentorships, workshops and seminars. After four years of this he expects you to out-earn most four-year graduates, often making money within the first year. [▶ 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dZ7xeVCYC5M)
- Staying broke is a choice over time: even a US minimum-wage worker earns over $1M in a lifetime and a median earner about $3M; the problem is where it goes. Roughly 35% of the average paycheck goes to lenders (mortgage, car, cards). Wealth is the ratio of what you earn to what you need; rule one is spend less than you make. [▶ 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ymFWgFiKUvM)
- Try a "buy nothing" challenge: unlink cards from shopping apps, leave your wallet at home, pay only fixed bills and discount groceries, pack lunch. He lived on under $15k/month while making $1M/month and kept $1,200 rent for years. [▶ 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ymFWgFiKUvM)
- Six-step plan (modeled on Dave Ramsey's baby steps): 1) starter emergency fund of $1k-5k before attacking debt; 2) pay off consumer debt using the quickest-to-clear-first order for psychological wins; 3) build 3-6 months of expenses in an interest-bearing account; 4) cut risky spending (turn in leases, buy a $5-10k used car in cash, go to one car); 5) invest 15% of pre-tax income automatically, plus up to another 15% in education; 6) pay off the mortgage. [▶ 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ymFWgFiKUvM)
- Price purchases in future value: $200 sneakers invested at about 9% for 40 years become roughly $6,000. Saving $250/month at 9% for 40 years reaches about $1M (so each extra $250/month is roughly another million); at a 4% withdrawal rate $2M supports about $80k/year. [▶ 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ymFWgFiKUvM)
- Translate fixed costs into workdays: on about $100/day after tax, a $600 lease eats 6 of 22 workdays and $1,200 rent another 12. Ask what you are willing to give up, not just what you will do. [▶ 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ymFWgFiKUvM)
- Want to be rich, not look rich: often the highest earners in his company lived paycheck to paycheck while others had more saved. Automate saving/investing, add friction to spending, and check accounts daily until savings are large. [▶ 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ymFWgFiKUvM)
- Extra $2,500/month from a side job or extra shifts invested in the S&P 500 from age 20 could compound to about $50M over 55 years; that money gets made either way, by you or by the banks. [▶ 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ymFWgFiKUvM)
- Investing in your earning capacity usually beats index returns: $10k in the market might return $1k, while $10k on a snowblower could take you from 3 driveways a day to 20. Pair the plan with a 30-day, 12-hour-a-day work challenge to prove you can do more. [▶ 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ymFWgFiKUvM)
- Invest in yourself over speculative assets: $10k in the index might earn about $900, while the same $10k on skills could raise income from $50k to $100k. He spent $10k of his $50k savings on a gym-owners mastermind before owning a gym and had his first location profitable and owner-independent by month nine. Paying for skills buys the future at a discount; he even relocated to be near better people in his field. [▶ 18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6KqndZuN_Yk)
- Prioritize being rich over looking rich, and always spend less than you make; outspending your income keeps you poor at any income level (he notes roughly half of Americans have no savings). [▶ 19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ySuYdJ0H4s)
- Price meetings: ten people earning $50k-$100k on a one-hour call cost roughly $400-500, like taking the team out to dinner several times a day; normalize leaving meetings where you add no value and remove makers and unnecessary managers from meetings. [▶ 20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GIRkQQHzsxI)
- Invest in what you understand: Ramsey's question to Graham Stephan (what share of your knowledge is real estate?) led Hormozi to put his post-exit capital into buying and growing businesses rather than buildings. Wealthy people Ramsey interviewed (a car dealer collecting classic cars, farmers buying land) put money in things they knew; most first-generation Forbes 400 members got rich through businesses, not 401(k)s. [▶ 21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jvXOOddDg_s)
- Debt adds risk that standard leverage math ignores; any number times zero is zero. Ramsey argues debt should be risk-adjusted like beta in fund analysis, comparing a business with debt against one without; both he and Hormozi operate debt-free, and Ramsey says cash let him ride out shocks. [▶ 21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jvXOOddDg_s)
- "Ignorance debt": if you earn $50K, you are effectively paying $950K a year for not knowing how to make $1M. Putting money into your own skills (e.g., a sales course that lifts income from $40K to $100K-220K) beats the roughly 10% a year from the S&P 500, and the gain repeats every year and stacks with each new skill, such as adding lead gen on top of sales. [▶ 22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Nh8Oc7ERdIU)
- Wealth alchemy: work out your cost per permanent customer. Example: $100 per trial, 1 in 3 trials converts, 1 in 3 customers stays permanently, so about $900 buys $1,200/yr of recurring revenue. At a 10x revenue multiple that is about $12K of enterprise value per customer. Spending $9M could create about $120M of untaxed asset value plus $12M/yr of revenue. [▶ 25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k-3PoOT4vOM)
- The first $100K in the bank is the biggest psychological unlock: it ends survival math (rent, phone, insurance) so you can think long term. He felt wealthier then than after his later exits. The target is $100K banked, not $100K in revenue. [▶ 27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk)
- Step 1, cut every cost so you can take more risk: no eating out, discount groceries only, no new clothes for about two years, cheapest possible housing (live with family or share a room; he paid $300-400/month), and a paid-off cheap car. [▶ 27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk)
- Grow active income first. Most self-made billionaires got there through large active income they could put at risk; rewards come from the risk you take, and you can't take risk without time and money. [▶ 27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk)
- Step 6, don't inflate your lifestyle. He kept his $400 shared room while earning about $20K/month, so the cash could fund new locations and learning. The day you stop spending on learning is the day you choose not to earn more. [▶ 27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk)
- Ignorance debt is the most expensive debt: what you should know but don't. You pay it down by failing, since an expert is someone who has made every mistake in a narrow field. Name the specific person whose judgment is stopping you (he nearly didn't sell Gym Launch at $46M over one colleague's opinion). [▶ 29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ub1D6RQocRU)
- Skills are income insurance. After losing everything, he made $100K the next month on a maxed-out credit card, which showed him that his skills, not the gyms, were the real asset. Investing in skills is a form of retirement plan. [▶ 31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ln24y0FPJHo)
- The first $100K is the hardest (it took him about 5 years). Focus on growing monthly income rather than the bank balance. Spending $2K to raise income from $5K to $6K/month pays back $12K a year. Foundations: own it, spend less than you make, and reinvest the surplus into earning more; you can't save your way out on minimum wage. [▶ 32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oys_fv25SYM)
- Failed experiments (a dead ad, a Shopify store) aren't a reset to zero; they're experience points that eventually level you up. The wealthiest people think in skills, and later they buy other people's skills and time by hiring. [▶ 32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oys_fv25SYM)
- Fortunes are made by taking big risks with small money and kept by taking small risks with big money. Education is the one asset no government, divorce or lawsuit can take; his family's experience fleeing Iran showed that skills survive when property doesn't. The "time tax of ignorance": not knowing how to make $1M/yr costs you $1M/yr. [▶ 35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JE2_7elAcxM)
- Maximizers beat optimizers: judge by absolute profit, not ratios. Spending $100 to make $1,000 (net $900) is worse than spending $200 to make $1,200 (net $1,000), even though ROI fell; you can 10x inputs, but you can never 10x a 30% opt-in rate. [▶ 42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0lMn_-EXyhQ)
- Use Buffett's test of price paid versus value received: the question is not whether a degree raises income but whether the increase is worth its total cost. [▶ 43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nxL4ZfVqKLI)
- He skipped Harvard Business School by comparing two years of no income plus $250K of debt against putting that money into starting a business, and found the business route taught more and paid more. [▶ 43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nxL4ZfVqKLI)
- Rich people use money to buy time, ambitious people use time to buy skills, and lazy people spend on distractions. Real generational wealth passes on as skills and education, not assets. [▶ 46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oDK4g5na4Jw)
- Acquisition.com was designed backward from "what could I do forever" (high leverage, compounding capital). It invests in businesses doing $3M+ (most over $5M, average around $17M), is slower and built on content-driven inbound, and exposure to many industries lets ideas cross-pollinate. [▶ 48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mqqbuM9sAk)
- "God mode": four teachers running 4-hour sessions bring in about $4,400 a day minus $800 in pay, about $3,600 a day of profit. A $1M/year income needs about $3,300 a day. [▶ 49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CGSd00h-6zI)
- The wealthiest people he knows spend less and look for ways to acquire things with little money out of pocket. [▶ 50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KNl83INePXI)
- Compare uses of $50K in savings: a 10% down payment on a $500K house (adding a mortgage liability) versus buying a local business that earns about $250K a year in profit, which jumps your income from about $60K to $250K. [▶ 50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KNl83INePXI)
- Rich people are more risk-averse because a single zero wipes out decades of good decisions; they buy things that can't go to zero, ideally for nothing down. Poor people buy lottery-like bets with near-certain loss. "You only have to get rich once." [▶ 50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KNl83INePXI)
- Underspend on status and overspend on education: flashy purchases impress no one who matters, and people further ahead respect you more for living lean and learning hard. [▶ 51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q6SdmgIji30)
- Don't simply save and index in your 20s: compound-interest projections ignore inflation (e.g. $4M in 60 years is roughly $1M today). Spending $10K to double or triple your earning power beats that, because you are your best asset. [▶ 51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q6SdmgIji30)
- Pay your learning fund first: move money off the top into a dedicated education account and let it build up until a worthwhile learning opportunity comes along, instead of spending what's left at month's end. [▶ 51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q6SdmgIji30)
- Automate investing and make spending manual (cash, separate accounts for rent, investing, food and car) so it's easy to invest and painful to spend. Never shop without a pre-approved list. [▶ 51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q6SdmgIji30)
- Price purchases in hours worked: at $20/hour after about 20% tax, a $100 shirt costs about 6 hours. At his $7.25/hour teen job, coworkers spent $15 of their ~$36 net daily pay on lunch. [▶ 51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q6SdmgIji30)
- Compete with yourself on how much you save and invest each month (your personal record), not on what you earn; he knows people earning millions who have nothing left. [▶ 51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q6SdmgIji30)
- Check your bank account every morning: facing reality is what lets you change it, much like weighing yourself daily. Spending on one-time experiences that only fit your 20s (e.g. backpacking Europe) is fine within limits, as long as it doesn't drain your investment account. [▶ 51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q6SdmgIji30)
- Borrow to buy an asset that others pay off: real estate is borrowed money plus tenants. A friend moved from house flips to buying a 14-unit building with other people's money, sold it four months later for $500K more, and then flipped 30-40 commercial buildings a year with just a couple of VAs. [▶ 52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7sLXhCDRaV8)
- Buy below value and refinance: contact enough owners (e.g. 1,000) and someone will sell well under market value. For example, put a $100K house under contract for $80K, have the seller finance part of it, and let the bank lend the rest, so you put no cash in and capture the gap. [▶ 52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7sLXhCDRaV8)
- Sell the contract: get a property under contract or an option below market (e.g. agree $800K with a long-time owner for a home worth about $1M), then assign it to an investor at $900K and keep the $100K spread without ever owning it. [▶ 52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7sLXhCDRaV8)
- Buy early from creators or companies with large audiences before launch or IPO; demand competing for a scarce item usually drives the price up later (how the NFT boom worked). This one does need some capital. [▶ 52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7sLXhCDRaV8)
- Two schools of investing: bettors (find mispriced companies and hold, Buffett-style) and builders (deploy templated playbooks and SOPs to grow companies 3-10x).
